lessons.title: Dynamic Programming Intuition
lessons.concept: Dynamic Programming (DP) solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results to avoid recomputation. It is useful when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.
lessons.formula: Two key properties: (1) overlapping subproblems, (2) optimal substructure. Approaches: top-down (memoization) and bottom-up (tabulation).
lessons.worked_example: Fibonacci: naive recursion recomputes F(2), F(3) many times. DP stores computed values so each F(i) is computed once.
mistakes: Using DP when subproblems do not overlap (plain divide-and-conquer may suffice)
Defining state incorrectly (missing parameters needed for subproblem)
Confusing greedy choices with DP optimal substructure

lessons.title: Memoization vs Tabulation
lessons.concept: Memoization is a top-down approach: write a recursive solution and cache results for states already solved. Tabulation is a bottom-up approach: solve smaller subproblems first and fill a table iteratively up to the target.
lessons.formula: Memoization: if state in cache return cache[state]; else compute, store, return. Tabulation: initialize base cases, iterate states in dependency order, compute dp[state].
lessons.worked_example: Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps): memoized function returns cached ways(n). Tabulation sets dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1 and computes dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2].
mistakes: Wrong base cases leading to incorrect table/recursion results
Iterating in wrong order in tabulation so dependencies are not ready
Forgetting to cache before returning in memoization

lessons.title: State, Transition, and Answer
lessons.concept: Designing a DP solution involves defining the state (what dp[i] represents), the transition (how to compute it from smaller states), and the final answer (which state/value to return). Clear definitions prevent off-by-one and logic errors.
lessons.formula: Template: State dp[i]=...; Transition dp[i]=f(dp[smaller states]); Base cases; Answer = dp[target] or max/min over states.
lessons.worked_example: Min cost to reach step i (conceptual): dp[i]=cost[i]+min(dp[i-1],dp[i-2]) with base cases dp[0]=cost[0], dp[1]=cost[1], answer=min(dp[n-1],dp[n-2]).
mistakes: Vague state meaning causing wrong transitions
Returning intermediate state instead of required final answer
